header:
Date: 2026-01-12, Time: 15:00 PT, Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Verdant CTO), Maya Patel (Verdant Lead Engineer), Samir Khan (Verdant SRE)
summary: AE + SE walked Verdant through Redwood SDK quickstarts (Python + TypeScript), authentication patterns (API key vs SSO), environment setup, and a recommended pilot plan. Discussed hosted vs Dedicated, security (SOC2, KMS), and next steps to run benchmarks and share docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we really appreciate you taking the time. Quick intros, I'm Alex AE on the Redwood team. Priya is our SE who will do most of the deep dive.
[00:12] Jordan Lee: Yep thanks Alex. Jordan here, CTO at Verdant, with Maya and Samir. We're looking at integrating Redwood for storefront personalization and search ranking. Want to cover quickstarts and auth.
[00:25] Priya Desai: Great, I'll share my screen and start with the Python quickstart. Bear with me while I open the SDK repo.
[00:35] [screen share starts]
[00:40] Priya Desai: So there's two packages we recommend, the official redwood-python SDK and the redwood-js client. In Python you pip install redwood-sdk, in TS npm i @redwoodai/sdk -- note sometimes the package name in the docs was redwood-client, sorry that was an older alias.
[00:58] Maya Patel: Quick Q, do we need a dedicated account or can we use hosted for the pilot? Our infra team is sensitive about PII.
[01:10] Priya Desai: For a pilot hosted is fine — you can isolate data retention and we support per-customer retention policies. If you need VPC or on-prem for compliance we'd look at Dedicated or Private deployment, that typically comes later.
[01:25] Alex Chen: Also to clarify the auth story: simplest is an API key set as REDWOOD_API_KEY in your environment. For stronger controls we integrate with your KMS and you can use short-lived tokens via our private deployment or Dedicated with KMS binding.
[01:40] Samir Khan: How does SSO fit? We use Okta for everything.
[01:45] Alex Chen: We support SAML/SSO for the Console and role-based access. For service-to-service workloads you still use API keys or our OIDC flow for short-lived credentials. We'll send the SSO guide.
[01:58] Priya Desai: Back to the quickstart — here's a tiny Python example: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.generate('prompt text', model='rw-instruct-1'); print(resp.text) — in the demo the generate call returns a streamable response and a sync response.
[02:30] [Jake? mislabeled speaker] Jordan Lee: Sorry did you say rw-instruct-1? Is that an internal model name?
[02:36] Priya Desai: Yeah we have model catalog entries like rw-instruct-1 and rw-chat-2, those are Redwood-verified build variants; we can map them to open models under the hood. If naming differs in the docs the console shows canonical names.
[02:50] Priya Desai: For TypeScript the snippet is import { Redwood } from '@redwoodai/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const r = await client.chat.create({ model: 'rw-chat-2', messages: [...] }); console.log(r.choices[0].message.content);
[03:10] Maya Patel: Do you support streaming in the JS SDK? We need low-latency updates for typing UX.
[03:15] Priya Desai: Yes both SDKs support streaming. In Node we use an event emitter pattern, in Python you can iterate over chunks. We'll share snippet with an SSE example.
[03:30] Samir Khan: What about local env setup? Our dev machines are locked down, so batch tests will run in CI — any specifics for CI tokens?
[03:40] Alex Chen: Best practice is to use project-level API keys scoped to non-prod environments, rotate them, and integrate with your secrets manager. For CI we recommend limited-scope tokens and IP allowlists; for Dedicated you get private networking.
[03:55] Jordan Lee: Can you show the Console quickly?
[04:00] [screen: Redwood Console]
[04:05] Priya Desai: Here is the Projects view, you can manage API keys, set routes, and pin model versions. The Optimize tab gives suggestions: it flagged this workload for batching (small prompt, high QPS) and recommends a quantization profile if memory bound.
[04:30] Maya Patel: We're sensitive about data residency. Can logs be restricted?
[04:35] Alex Chen: Yes, we support configurable retention, customer-managed S3 exports, and audit logs. For Private deployments your logs never leave your VPC unless you opt in. We'll attach the SOC2 and data residency docs.
[04:52] [transcription note: "S3" sometimes transcribed as "S three"]
[05:00] Priya Desai: Now I'll walk through a local quickstart. Step 1: pip install, set env var REDWOOD_API_KEY, run python quickstart.py. The quickstart uses a tiny prompt set and demonstrates prefix caching by sending same prefix twice to show cache hits.
[05:22] Jordan Lee: How does caching interact with privacy? We cannot cache customer PII.
[05:28] Priya Desai: Good point. Caching can be disabled per-route and sensitive routes should use no-cache. We also support token scrubbing and request filters before anything is persisted.
[05:40] Maya Patel: Are there SDK examples for embeddings / similarity search?
[05:44] Priya Desai: Yep, both SDKs include embeddings helpers. Python: client.embeddings.create(model='rw-embed-1', inputs=[...]) returns vectors you can push to your vector DB or to Redwood's managed store. We'll share the sample repo that shows a small vector search example.
[06:05] Samir Khan: Performance — what's the typical latency? We aim < 200ms p95 for short prompts.
[06:12] Alex Chen: For hosted that depends on model and batch size. With our optimized kernels smaller instruction models often hit <100ms token latency, but 200ms p95 for full generation is common target. For strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated with pinned capacity and warm KV caches. We'll run a benchmark with your dataset.
[06:35] Maya Patel: For the benchmark, we'll need a checklist of what you need from us.
[06:40] Priya Desai: We'll need anonymized prompt samples, expected concurrency/QPS, target latency and quality criteria, and any special constraints (e.g., must avoid external network calls). Jordan, can you share the prompts and QPS?
[06:52] Jordan Lee: Yes we'll pull an anonymized set and share by next week.
[06:56] [crosstalk as screen changes]
[07:05] Priya Desai: A couple gotchas: 1) If you use serverless at high QPS, request tail latencies can spike because of cold KV caches — we recommend warmup run. 2) Make sure you pin model versions via the Console if you want reproducible outputs.
[07:25] Maya Patel: Do you have a Terraform provider for infra and route creation?
[07:29] Alex Chen: We have a CLI and a Terraform provider in beta. We'll share the provider link. It's useful for provisioning API keys and routes as code.
[07:40] Jordan Lee: Any concerns integrating with our existing vector DB (we use Pinecone)?
[07:44] Priya Desai: No issue. You can use Redwood embeddings and store vectors in Pinecone. If you want managed nearest-neighbor we can discuss Redwood-managed vector store as an option.
[07:55] Samir Khan: About security: KMS — do you support customer-managed keys?
[08:00] Alex Chen: Yes for Dedicated/Private you can bind to your KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and we support HSM-backed keys for highest assurance. We'll send the KMS integration doc.
[08:12] Maya Patel: Is there an offline testing mode? We want to run smoke tests without calling production endpoints.
[08:18] Priya Desai: There's a local mock server in the sample repo that returns canned responses. For more realistic benching we recommend a separate staging project in Redwood with dedicated capacity or a lower-cost model.
[08:30] Jordan Lee: Pricing — rough ballpark for pilot?
[08:33] Alex Chen: For pilot we usually recommend hosted usage; if you keep QPS modest cost is usage-based. For Dedicated we can provide an estimate based on committed GPUs and target throughput. I'll follow up with a tailored estimate after we get your QPS.
[08:48] Maya Patel: Anything else we should be aware of re: SDK versions?
[08:52] Priya Desai: Keep SDK pinned to a minor version in your lockfile. We ship client deprecations with a 3-month window and the Console will alert you to breaking changes.
[09:05] [longer pause as Priya pulls up sample repo]
[09:20] Priya Desai: I'm going to demo a short TypeScript integration: we create a serverless function using Vercel / Netlify that reads REDWOOD_API_KEY from env and calls client.chat.create, shows streaming back to the browser. Key point: keep secrets out of client-side bundles.
[09:45] Maya Patel: For streaming to browser, do you recommend using a Backend-for-Frontend?
[09:49] Priya Desai: Yes, BFF or edge function that handles auth is recommended. Never expose API keys directly in the browser.
[09:56] Jordan Lee: Onboarding — how long to get from pilot to production?
[09:59] Alex Chen: Typical timeline is 4–8 weeks from pilot to production for teams that have clear success criteria. If Dedicated or Private is required add procurement time, usually 6–10 weeks depending on network setup.
[10:15] Samir Khan: Can you recap action items?
[10:19] Alex Chen: Sure — we'll send Python/TS snippets and the sample repo; we'll attach SOC2 + KMS docs; schedule bench week of Jan 18; provide pricing estimate.
[10:30] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. Maya, Samir — we'll coordinate test data.
[10:36] Maya Patel: Yep, I'll start pulling prompts and anonymizing.
[10:40] Alex Chen: Great thanks everyone, we'll email the links and next steps.
[10:45] [meeting ends]

Notes: transcript has occasional mis-attributions and small transcription errors (package names, model IDs may appear slightly different than Console). Shared artifacts: quickstart repo link (https://github.com/redwoodai/quickstarts/tree/main/sdk), SOC2 whitepaper link (internal doc), Terraform provider beta link.
